title: The first twenty-one words
hookLine: metta, the breath, dukkha, the Buddha, the four truths, sati, anicca, anatta, dana, karuna, sangha, upekkha, the middle way
tomorrow: can a verse you picked years ago still fit you now?

cards: A phone slips and the screen cracks. That's one hit. Then come the hours after: why did I put it there, I always do this, everything I touch breaks.
Mai knows the feeling this week. Her senior show opened, and a passing backpack tore the corner of her best piece. The tear took a second.
The replay took all night, every angle, every what-if. The Buddha has a name for that replay. He calls it the second arrow.

teach.b: In the sutta, a person who hasn't trained feels a painful feeling, and then grieves, laments, beats the chest, grows distraught.
It's as if, the Buddha says, someone were struck by an arrow, and then struck by a second arrow right after it. Two pains.

teach.h: THE TRAINED STILL FEEL THE FIRST.
teach.b: The trained disciple feels the first arrow too. The sutta never says they don't. But they don't fire the second one.
And the text adds something sharp: the untrained person, hurting, runs to pleasure, because they know no other way out.
Now look at the first words of this path, from five years ago, because they were built for exactly this. Dukkha: the first arrow is real; name it. The breath: the place to come back to.
Sati: mindfulness, seeing the second arrow being drawn. Anicca: this pain changes too. Upekkha: steadiness, so the mind doesn't tip over.
Metta: kindness, turned on yourself, and on whoever's backpack it was. Karuna: compassion, for everyone who has ever watched something they made get damaged.
Dana: giving, even just your attention, back to the people who came to see the work.
The middle way: no pretending it didn't hurt, no drowning in it.
The first words weren't vocabulary. They were tools. Five years ago they were new words.
On a bad day, they're the ones within reach.

how: Buddhist teachers often use the simile of the two arrows (SN 36.6) when teaching how to meet pain: feel the first, and notice the added grief, worry and blame as a second arrow that practice can set down.

games.q: what does “the first twenty-one words” mean?
o: the path's opening vocabulary, met again as tools
the oldest words the Buddha ever spoke aloud
the vows a monk recites on the day he is ordained

games.q: the first words as tools — tap the pairs.
p: the first arrow is real: name it
seeing the second arrow being drawn
steady, so the mind doesn't tip

s: in the sutta, a trained disciple feels no pain at all
the first arrow still lands; it's the second the trained one doesn't add.
the sutta says a hurting, untrained person runs to pleasure as the only way out they know
that's the text's sharp detail: pleasure as the only escape they know.

games.q: your teammate misses the winning shot, then spends the bus ride saying she's useless at everything. using the two arrows, what do you say?
o: the miss hurt, and that's real. 'i'm useless' is a second arrow; that one you can put down.
don't feel anything about it; being upset is just attachment.
it wasn't your fault at all; blame the ref and forget it.
games.why: in the sutta the trained disciple still feels the first arrow. the second, the grief piled on top, is the one practice lets you skip.

practice: Say the first words out loud, slowly, one on each breath out: metta, the breath, dukkha, the Buddha, the four truths, sati, anicca, anatta, dana, karuna, sangha, upekkha, the middle way.
If one of them catches on something from your week, stay on it for a few breaths before you go on.

wordCard.voice: The first twenty-one words: the path's opening vocabulary, and, it turns out, its first-aid kit.

orig.note: Pali: arrow, dart; the sutta is called the Sallatha, the arrow.

carryVoice: For the road: the first words, still the right tools for a bad day. See you tomorrow.
